summary: This document describes a threat model for the setting in which External BGP path security mechanisms will be developed. It analyzes the RPKI and focuses on an Autonomous System's ability to verify the authenticity of the AS path information it receives.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building a lock, you ask who might try to break in and how. This lists the ways someone could lie about the route a message takes across the Internet.

questions: how can as path be forged
subtitle: Who might attack BGP paths and the RPKI behind them, and what protections cannot stop.

tldr.problem: BGP has no way for an AS to verify that the AS_PATH in a route it receives is genuine, and a design to fix that has to know which adversaries and attacks it is meant to withstand.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five classes of adversary (network operators, hackers, criminals, registries and nations) and classifies attacks on routers, management computers, repository publication points and RPKI certification authorities.
tldr.outcome: It ends with residual vulnerabilities that path security cannot remove, including route leaks, unprotected attributes and failure to withdraw routes.

today: RFC 7132 is an Informational RFC published in February 2014, and its metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC. It states that it should be revised if the SIDR security context later grows to cover route leaks or other BGP attributes.

sections.title: What PATHSEC Must Protect
sections.content:
PATHSEC means any design that preserves the integrity and authenticity of the AS_PATH attribute in a BGP update message. This RFC deliberately avoids the name BGPSEC, which other documents use for one specific design. The goal is to let a BGP speaker verify that the ASes listed in the path are the sequence of ASes the route actually traversed.

The security context comes from the SIDR working group charter. Solutions must use the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), and must protect only what is needed to verify the path and that the NLRI is what was advertised. The model has no "oracle" that sees all BGP inputs and outputs. It is AS-centric, based on a local notion of legitimate behavior. Attacks on unprotected BGP are not revisited, since BGP-4 already covers them.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet networks pass along directions like a game of telephone. The goal is to let a network check that nobody changed the list of stops along the way.

sections.title: Adversaries and Threats
sections.content:
The RFC defines a threat as a motivated, capable adversary. An adversary who lacks motive or capability is not a threat. Five classes are considered.

  • Network operators control their own BGP routers and can make them emit inaccurate routes, for example to steer traffic along paths that favor them.
  • Hackers may take over operators' routers or management computers, but are assumed generally unable to mount man-in-the-middle attacks on most links.
  • Criminals may extort operators or telecom staff, or manipulate routing to hide the source of spam or DoS attacks.
  • Registries can manipulate repository content or mismanage certificates.
  • Nations may control operators or registries, or wiretap inter-network traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five kinds of troublemakers: the mapmakers themselves, sneaky hackers, criminals, the people who hand out addresses, and whole countries. Each can do different things.

sections.title: Attacks on Routers and Sessions
sections.content:
An active attacker may target the BGP (TCP) session between two routers, for instance by replaying or modifying messages. This RFC does not address those attacks further, because RFC 4272 describes countermeasures, and protecting inter-router links is outside the scope of PATHSEC.

Attacks on a router include AS insertion, false route origination (addressed by the RPKI), secure path downgrade (removing path data from a protected update), invalid path data, stale announcements, a compromised router private key and withdrawal suppression. Behavior that could be explained by local policy, such as failing to propagate a withdrawal or causing a route leak, is not treated as an attack, because PATHSEC cannot detect it as unauthorized.
sections.plainLanguage: A cheating router might add a fake stop to a list or remove a real one. Some bad behavior, like not passing on news that a road closed, looks the same as an honest choice, so it cannot be called cheating.

sections.title: Attacks on the RPKI
sections.content:
PATHSEC relies on the RPKI, so the RFC covers attacks on it. An attacker who compromises an operator's management computers could delete objects at its publication point, request revocation of certificates, or change the origin AS in Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs). Externally this looks like rogue operator behavior.

An attacker who only controls a repository host cannot forge signatures, so the attacks become denial of service against relying parties. Relying parties keep a local cache, and a manifest lets them detect deleted objects. Replacing a manifest with an older one makes it stale, which is also detectable. A compromised CA can do more: revoke or replace certificates, issue overlapping resources, or flood relying parties with many ROAs or very short validity times. The extensions in RFC 3779 stop a compromised CA from issuing valid certificates for resources outside its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory of who owns which addresses can be vandalized. Because everything in it is signed, fakes are caught, but tearing pages out is harder to prevent, so everyone keeps a copy.

sections.title: Residual Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
Some weaknesses remain. If a relying party sees stale or missing repository data, it can keep using its cache, which exposes it to attacks that rely on its ignorance of changes. It can instead purge expired objects, which moves those resources into the unprotected set and lets an attacker move them out of protection. A CA can also misbehave within its own resources, for example by issuing duplicate allocations.

PATHSEC itself has three listed gaps. Route leaks are out of scope, because BGP has no semantics that preclude them and no RFC defines the term. Attributes other than the path need not be protected. And PATHSEC cannot ensure that an AS withdraws a route it no longer has, though lifetime limits on advertisements bound how long that failure lasts.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a good lock leaves some gaps. The system cannot stop a network from lying about taking a road off the map, but it can make old information expire.

items.title: Network operators
items.text: Control routers and can emit inaccurate routes.

items.title: Hackers
items.text: Remote attackers who may take over operator systems.

items.title: Criminals
items.text: May extort operators or hide the source of abuse.

items.title: Registries
items.text: Can manipulate repository content or certificates.

items.title: Nations
items.text: May control operators or registries, or wiretap links.
